solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Durham’s foremost dons translated Horace with variable use of improvisation

indicators.note: takes the first letter of Durham
Horace's letters are rendered into a new form

explanation.surface: University dons in Durham turn out a translation of the Latin poet Horace, improvising as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: The D goes inside AHOCER+Y, between the first and second letters. 'Dons' looks like the academics; it is the verb 'puts on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Adhocery is the habit of making things up as you go along, using ad hoc measures.

clue.text: Regrettably snubbed theology graduate during panto

indicators.note: a snub nose is cut short, so ALAS loses its tail

blocks.note: ALAS (regrettably) with its last letter cut off

explanation.surface: Sadly, a divinity graduate was ignored while watching a pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: A panto (pantomime) is the British Christmas stage show for families; Aladdin is one of the classic stories. 'Snubbed' looks like 'ignored' but means shortened.
explanation.definitionFit: Aladdin is one of the best-known pantomimes staged at Christmas.

clue.text: Stifling each other’s essential characters

indicators.note: the answer comes from the inner letters of the phrase

blocks.note: the last letter of 'each' and first two of 'other' sit together in the middle of the phrase

explanation.surface: Each person smothering the other's true nature.
explanation.walkthrough: The word 'essential' suggests core personality; here it means the letters at the heart of 'each other'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: stifling air is so hot it smothers you.

clue.text: Unhappily recording second of many errors

indicators.note: the letters sit badly and must be rearranged
take the second letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A sad recording captures the second of many mistakes.
explanation.walkthrough: Corrigenda are strictly errors to be corrected, the list printed at the end of a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Corrigenda are errors, especially printing errors listed for correction.

clue.text: One sent to Coventry returned in disgust

indicators.note: sent back, so the word is read backwards

blocks.note: to send someone to Coventry is to shun them; a leper is a shunned outcast

explanation.surface: An outcast came back home in disgust.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Send to Coventry' is a British idiom for refusing to speak to someone; Coventry is an English city.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: what repels you revolts or disgusts you, driving you back.

clue.text: Carefully considers idiosyncrasies in speech

indicators.note: the word is spoken, not written

blocks.note: someone's little ways are their quirks

explanation.surface: Someone scrutinises the odd habits of a speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In speech' seems to locate the quirks in someone's talk; it is the sound signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To weigh a matter is to consider it carefully.

clue.text: Exhausted employees having to keep working for ages

indicators.note: emptied, so only the outer letters remain
the outer letters hold the next piece inside

blocks.note: employees with the middle emptied out
a machine that is on is working

explanation.surface: Worn-out staff are made to carry on working for a very long time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Exhausted' looks like tired; it means emptied of the inner letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Eons are ages, vast spans of time.

clue.text: Cook festive goose after swapping tips

indicators.note: the first letters of the two words change places

blocks.note: a gander is a male goose

explanation.surface: A Christmas recipe: roast a goose after trimming its ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cook' sounds like the kitchen, but it means rig, as in cooking the books.
explanation.definitionFit: To gerrymander is to rig electoral boundaries, which is to cook them.

clue.text: Exude mystery and energy

blocks.note: E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: Give off an air of enigma and vitality.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a description of charisma; the first word is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, from biology: glands secrete, or ooze out, their fluids.

clue.text: New programs bolstering school spirit

indicators.note: a bolster supports from inside, so the new programs sit within

explanation.surface: Fresh initiatives are boosting morale at a school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'School spirit' reads as morale; the phrase splits, and spirit is the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit by example: schnapps is a strong clear liquor from Germany and Scandinavia.

clue.text: Focusing on man lost on incorrect path

indicators.note: the letters have lost their way and wander into a new order

explanation.surface: A man has strayed from the right road and is lost.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' seems to be the one who is lost, but it belongs to the definition; 'incorrect' is fodder, not the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthropocentric means treating humankind as the centre of everything.

clue.text: School field

blocks.note: as a verb, to school is to train or drill someone
a field of study, an academic subject

explanation.walkthrough: 'School' is a verb here, to train, not the building; the answer means both training and a branch of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Discipline means both training (to school) and a branch of knowledge (a field).

clue.text: Considerable gin is in fact drunk

indicators.note: the letters stagger into a new order

explanation.surface: A lot of gin has in fact been drunk.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a boozy confession; its last word is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Significant means considerable in amount or importance.

clue.text: Limits of glossary concerning literary circle

indicators.note: take the outermost letters of the next word

blocks.note: first and last letters of glossary

explanation.surface: The boundaries of a glossary compiled for a literary society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Literary circle' looks like a book club; it is a circle found in literature, the gyre of Yeats's poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Gyre is a literary word for a circle or spiral, used by Yeats ('Turning and turning in the widening gyre').

clue.text: Revolutionary who was French polisher and athlete

blocks.note: Jean-Paul Marat of the French Revolution
one who hones, sharpening or polishing

explanation.surface: A French revolutionary who took up French polishing and running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French polisher' is a real trade (a wood-finisher), but 'French' belongs to Marat.
explanation.definitionFit: A marathoner is an athlete who runs marathons.

clue.text: Ignore information about the French court

blocks.note: gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: Disregard what you have heard about the French royal court.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information, as in 'getting the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to leave something unattended, to pay it no heed.

clue.text: Cross nationalist from south India cooked over charcoal

indicators.note: in a down clue, read from the bottom up

blocks.note: a rood is a cross, as in rood screen
India is I in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An angry nationalist from southern India, and some barbecue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' looks like angry; it is the noun, a rood. 'From south' belongs to the reversal, not to India.
explanation.definitionFit: Tandoori food is cooked in a tandoor, a clay oven heated by charcoal.

clue.text: Quiet about breaking false teeth

blocks.note: a dental plate holds false teeth

explanation.surface: Some teeth got smashed and nobody made a fuss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quiet' is a verb, to calm someone, not the adjective. CA is short for circa, Latin for about.
explanation.definitionFit: A verb sense of quiet: to calm an angry person down.

clue.text: Front of cabin covered and carpeted

indicators.note: the front of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: The front of a cabin has been covered and laid with carpet.
explanation.walkthrough: To be carpeted is British informal for being called in and told off, not having a floor covering.
explanation.definitionFit: Chidden is the old past participle of chide: scolded, or carpeted.

clue.text: Risked neck, regularly fleeing English country houses

indicators.note: every other letter departs, leaving N and C
the country holds the other letters inside it

blocks.note: Chad is a country in Africa
alternate letters of neck: N, C

explanation.surface: Someone stuck their neck out escaping from English stately homes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Risked neck' looks like one phrase; the definition is just 'Risked'. Chad is the African country.
explanation.definitionFit: To chance something is to risk it.

clue.text: Throw mud at faceless Samoan?

indicators.note: the first letter, the face, is removed

blocks.note: a Samoan is, for example, an islander

explanation.surface: Sling mud at a Pacific islander who has lost face.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that a Samoan is just one example of an islander. Remove the I to leave SLANDER.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: to throw mud is to smear someone's name with false charges.

clue.text: Get sick again close to Khyber Pass

indicators.note: takes the last letter of the next word

explanation.surface: Falling ill again near the Khyber Pass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Khyber Pass' reads as the mountain route; the phrase splits, and 'Pass' is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To relapse is to fall ill again after recovering.

clue.text: Undisturbed hiding place for drug

explanation.surface: A quiet stash where someone keeps narcotics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hiding place' looks like one phrase; split it, and 'hiding' is the removal signal working on 'place'.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: acid is the street name for LSD.

clue.text: Instrument about to capture this female nutritional need

explanation.surface: A musical instrument is about to catch a woman who needs feeding.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to' reads as 'on the point of'; split it, as 'about' is the container signal and 'to capture' is COP.
explanation.definitionFit: Tocopherol is vitamin E, a nutrient the body needs.

clue.text: Love mum’s ace raw tripe

blocks.note: A is ace on playing cards

explanation.surface: Darling, your mother's uncooked tripe is excellent.
explanation.walkthrough: Omasa (singular omasum) are the third stomachs of cattle and other ruminants; one of the stomachs sold as tripe.
explanation.definitionFit: The omasum is a ruminant's third stomach, eaten as tripe; raw means before it is cooked.

clue.text: Soldiers occupy a position around river

indicators.note: turned around, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: to be somewhere is to occupy a position

explanation.surface: Troops take up position around a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like a container signal; it turns the whole phrase back. The Ebro is a Spanish river.
explanation.definitionFit: A river by example: the Ebro flows across north-east Spain to the Mediterranean.

clue.text: Ex-PM’s fashionable royal post

blocks.note: Neville Chamberlain, British Prime Minister 1937–40, with 's

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister's stylish job at the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: Neville Chamberlain was a British Prime Minister. The Lord Chamberlain is a senior official of the royal household.
explanation.definitionFit: A chamberlainship is the office of chamberlain, a post in a royal household.

clue.text: Bears and hyenas scratching itch

indicators.note: to scratch a runner is to withdraw it

blocks.note: letters from which YEN is removed
a yen is an itch, a craving

explanation.surface: Wild animals scratch at an itch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bears' looks like the animal alongside hyenas; it is the verb, carries or has.
explanation.definitionFit: To bear a name or a mark is to have it.

clue.text: Some flipped, reportedly unwelcome

indicators.note: only part of the next word is used
the letters are read backwards

explanation.surface: Some people apparently flipped, saying they felt unwanted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reportedly' looks like a sound signal; here it is the word that hides the letters. De trop is French for 'too much', borrowed into English.
explanation.definitionFit: De trop means not wanted, in the way, unwelcome.

clue.text: Just read out passage in knitting pattern

indicators.note: spoken, so the sound matters rather than the spelling

explanation.surface: Simply read out a passage from a knitting pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: Fair Isle is a Shetland island that gave its name to a style of multicoloured knitting.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair Isle is a traditional pattern of coloured bands in knitting.
